Film: *Teaching to See*, directed by Andrei Severny, produced by Edward Tufte,
on the teaching of designer Inge Druckrey (37 min).

---

## Opening impression

The image that stayed with me was the Beethoven poster, where the letter **E**
is drawn together with the lines of a musical staff. I did not see the staff at
first; it appeared only after I had been looking for a while. That is the point
of the film in one image: visual design is not decoration handed to the viewer
all at once. Some things have to be looked at for a while before the details
come out. Druckrey trains exactly this kind of looking.

## 1. Thin/thick and curve/linearity

The exercises focus on the thick and thin parts of a letter. At first I did not
understand why a stroke would be thicker at the ends and thinner in the middle,
but the result looks balanced and calm rather than stiff. The variation comes
from the writing tool: a broad pen held at a fixed angle produces a wide mark
in one direction and a narrow one in the other, so the thickness of a curve
changes continuously as it turns. Where a straight stem meets a curve, that
transition has to be smoothed by hand, or the letter looks broken. Redrawing
the same letter many times is how the students learn to feel where the weight
should go.

The work is also about **space**, not only about the strokes themselves. The Roman alphabet is remarkably symmetrical, and when the
students modify an existing typeface, every letter has to be adjusted so that
the spaces inside and between the letters stay even. Design has to leave room.

## 2. The eye and the hand

Holmes separates writing into two opposing aspects. The eye is the conservative
one: "the eye wants to look at an orderly set of marks on a page — the eye wants
pattern," something regular and reliable. The hand is "the radical aspect of
writing": it wants to move, and to "write faster and faster." Writing is the
negotiation between them.

A signature is where that tension becomes visible. It is produced too quickly
for the eye to impose order on it, so what remains is the trace of the hand —
which is exactly why a signature is unique and hard to forget. The letterform
exercises in the film work in the opposite direction: they slow the hand down
until the eye can lead.

## 3. Calligraphy, Steve Jobs, and the Macintosh

Jobs took a calligraphy class, and the film connects that class to the
typography of the Macintosh. What he learned was not only that letters can be
beautiful. Calligraphy teaches judgment about proportion, spacing, and the
small visual corrections that make a line of text read well. When the Macintosh
shipped with proportionally spaced fonts and careful letterforms, it carried
that judgment into a machine, and from there into everything that was made with
it.

## 4. Geometric accuracy versus optical accuracy

Geometric accuracy and optical accuracy are not the same thing. A letter can be
measured and constructed so that every dimension is exactly equal, and it will
still look wrong to the eye — a little heavy here, a little short there. The eye
does not measure; it compares, and it is easily misled by shape. So the designer
deliberately introduces small deviations from the geometry until the letter
*looks* right, and at that point the viewer accepts it as correct without
noticing that anything was changed.

The thinning of a stem toward its middle, which I described above, is one of
these corrections: geometrically the stroke is no longer of even width, but
optically it reads as straighter and steadier than a stroke of constant width.

The same judgment governs the alphabet as a whole. In the film the students work
toward three things at once. First, the letters have to **share a common
structure**, so that they read as one alphabet rather than a collection of
separate drawings. Second, each letter has to stay **different enough from every
other letter** to remain legible — the shared structure cannot be pushed so far
that an *a* starts to look like an *o*. Third, the **spacing between letters**
has to produce an even rhythm and an even color on the page.

Spacing is the clearest case of optical over geometric accuracy. Equal measured
gaps do not look equal, because the shapes on either side differ: the space
between two straight stems and the space beside a round or diagonal letter are
measured the same and seen differently. The spacing is therefore set by eye
until the line of text has an even texture, not by making the distances equal.

This is why Druckrey's students correct their letters by eye rather than by
ruler. Being measurably right is not the goal; being read correctly is.

## What this means for data visualization

Druckrey's students spend hours on one letter, redrawing it and adjusting the
space around it. That is the same work we do when we choose an axis range, a
color, or how much white space a chart gets. In both cases the measurement is
not the goal — being read correctly is. A chart can be geometrically accurate,
with every value plotted exactly, and still be read wrongly, in the same way
that a geometrically perfect letter can look wrong. Anscombe's quartet is the
statistical version of the same lesson, and the bubble chart I critiqued in
Assignment 1 is the visual one: the circles were scaled correctly by area, yet
readers still could not see how much the banks had lost.

Learning to see is learning to check what the reader's eye actually receives,
not what the number says should be there.
